newsitem.title: USA: Telescope deployed by shuttle starts work.
newsitem.headline: Telescope deployed by shuttle starts work.

text.p: A telescope deployed from the space shuttle Columbia began probing the heavens on Thursday as the astronauts checked out their spacewalking gear.

The Orfeus-Spas telescope, set free from Columbia on Tuesday night, began observations that will provide astronomers with new information on the mysterious interstellar medium that occupies the space between the stars.

"Characterizing the composition and physical state of this gas tells us about the life cycle of the stars and also their influence on their environment," said Edward Jenkins a principal investigator for one of the telescope's instruments.
The interstellar matter accounts for about a quarter of the mass of the Milky Way galaxy and is the matter from which stars form.
Among the first targets for the U.S.-German telescope were halo stars located far from the galaxy's disc and a white dwarf star, hotter than our own sun but the same size as the earth.

Aboard Columbia, 28 miles (45 km) ahead of the telescope, astronauts Tammy Jernigan and Tom Jones floated in a jumble of spacesuit parts, testing the gear they will wear for a pair of spacewalks, the first of which is scheduled for Thanksgiving night.

During the six-hour sorties into the shuttle's cargo bay, the astronauts will practice assembly of the international space station. They will test a 17-foot (5.2 metre) manually operated crane for moving large space-station components.
The shuttle crew also planned to check the Wake Shield Facility, an orbiting semiconductor factory, being flown aboard the shuttle for the third time.

The saucer-shaped craft will be lifted into space by the shuttle's 60-foot (18.3 metre) robot arm on Friday evening. The spacecraft's designers said they have solved the technical problems that plagued its earlier flights.
The device will employ the vacuum of space to manufacture ultra-pure components for the electronics industry.
The astronauts tried without any luck to catch a glimpse of an Atlas rocket as it blasted off from Cape Canaveral Air Station on Thursday afternoon.
"We were watching the vicinty of the Cape for any smoke trails but didn't see any," said shuttle skipper Ken Cockrell.
The clean-burning rocket, which leaves little exhaust, carried a European television satellite into orbit.
